submission.natural_language_explanation: N2133+ fires on the language of making, supporting or contesting a claim: the epistemic vocabulary in which a text states what is known, argued, assumed, disputed or in doubt (evidence, hypothesis, premise, criteria, valid/invalid, claim, submit, confirm, conclude, dispute, cause, 'not true'), and, in scientific, medical and legal writing, on the specialist term such a claim is made about (autosomal, meningitidis, falciparum, indisputable, aneurysm), with the peak on that word or on the function word introducing it, usually at its first sub-word chunk. It stays at its GELU floor on narrative, dialogue, instructions, plain description, sports reporting and simple promotional copy that make no claim, even when those contain the same learned words used descriptively or evaluatively ('the plot is linear', 'the company's prognosis', 'dedicated counsel', 'she read the diagnosis'); a single learned word or one bare general sentence ('every case is different') is not enough, so the clause needs a run of claim or specialist-assertion language.

Groundwater in the lower valley moves slowly through layered sand and gravel, and in places it takes more than forty years for water to travel from the recharge zone to the wells that supply the towns along the river. The regional board began sampling private wells in the spring of 2011, and by the end of the decade it had assembled a record of nitrate concentrations from more than nine hundred sites. Field crews drew samples from kitchen taps, sealed them in chilled coolers and shipped them to a laboratory, where each bottle was analysed within its holding time. The resulting dataset describes a clear pattern: concentrations are highest beneath the older orchards, where fertiliser was applied heavily for decades, and lowest under the grazing land at the northern edge of the basin. Recharge during wet winters pushes the plume slowly downward, and the leading edge of the highest concentrations has moved perhaps two hundred metres in twenty years.

The board published a first draft of its action plan in March, and the document ran to more than three hundred pages. It described the geology, the sampling methods, the laboratory results and the projected cost of replacing affected wells. It also proposed a limit of ten milligrams per litre for new wells, a figure taken from the national drinking-water standard rather than from any local study, and it suggested that growers in the hot spots move to a slower-release fertiliser over five years. Public meetings were held in three towns, and the transcripts run to several hundred pages of testimony from growers, residents, engineers and the district's own hydrologists.

It was in the technical appendix that the argument became sharp. The board's consultants assert that the measured concentrations are rising faster than any plausible change in farming practice can explain, and they conclude that the legacy store of nitrate in the unsaturated zone, rather than current application rates, is the dominant cause of what the wells now draw. The growers' hydrologist disputes that premise. He argues that the monitoring wells are screened at depths which mix old water with new, that the sampling network was never designed to detect trends, and that the consultants' model cannot be tested against any observation made before 1990. His submission states that the ten-milligram figure is arbitrary, that it has never been subjected to independent review, and that the criteria the board used to select its hot spots were altered midway through the process without explanation. The board's reply concedes that the network has limits but maintains that the direction of travel is not in doubt, and it cites two outside studies which it says confirm the consultants' reading. Neither side has produced evidence the other accepts, and the hearing officer has asked both parties to file a joint statement setting out the points that remain in dispute before the plan can be adopted.

Residents who came to the meetings mostly asked about their own wells. They wanted to know whether the water was safe to drink, what a filter would cost, and whether the board would pay for testing. Staff answered what they could and promised to publish a map of the affected parcels by the end of the year. The map appeared in December, and it shows that nearly a third of the sampled parcels lie inside the proposed hot spots. Whether that finding is valid depends on assumptions nobody has yet tested, and the board has said it will not act until the joint statement is filed and the disputed criteria are settled.
